commands.name: terraform init
commands.summary: Initialize a Terraform working directory and download providers.
commands.risk_reason: Downloads providers from internet; modifies .terraform directory.
commands.explanation: terraform init initializes the working directory: downloads provider plugins, sets up the backend for state storage, and installs modules. Must be run before any other Terraform commands and after any backend or provider changes.

flags.desc: Upgrade providers to latest matching version constraints

examples.desc: Upgrade providers to latest allowed versions
Init with external backend config (for secrets)

commands.pro_tip: Use `terraform init -backend-config=backend.hcl` to keep backend credentials (S3 bucket, DynamoDB table names) out of version-controlled Terraform files — a required practice for security.

commands.name: terraform plan
commands.summary: Preview changes Terraform will make to infrastructure.
commands.risk_reason: Read-only by default; saves a plan file that can be applied.
commands.explanation: terraform plan compares desired state (HCL) with current state (tfstate) and shows exactly what will be created, changed, or destroyed. Always run before apply — the plan output is your contract for what will happen in production.

flags.desc: Save plan to a file for later apply

commands.pro_tip: In CI/CD, always use `terraform plan -out=tfplan` then `terraform apply tfplan` — the saved plan ensures apply executes exactly what was reviewed, preventing drift between plan and apply.

commands.name: terraform apply
commands.summary: Apply Terraform changes to provision or update infrastructure.
commands.risk_reason: Creates, modifies, or destroys real infrastructure and may incur costs.
cautions: Changes real infrastructure and can destroy resources — read every line marked “destroy” or “must be replaced”.
Check the workspace and backend first (terraform workspace show); the wrong one targets the wrong environment.
Never use -auto-approve outside throw-away environments or a CI job applying a reviewed plan.
commands.explanation: terraform apply executes the changes shown by terraform plan. Without -auto-approve, it shows the plan and waits for confirmation. When passed a saved plan file, it applies exactly that plan. Changes are recorded in the state file.

flags.desc: Skip state refresh (faster, use with caution)

safer.why: Create a saved plan and review it.
Apply exactly the plan you reviewed.

commands.pro_tip: Never use `-auto-approve` without a saved plan file (`-auto-approve tfplan`) in production — always know exactly what you're auto-approving. Save the plan, review it, then apply it.

commands.name: ansible
commands.summary: Run one-off Ansible tasks on remote hosts without a playbook.
commands.risk_reason: Executes commands on remote hosts; verify host patterns carefully.
cautions: Ad-hoc shell/command modules run on every matched host in parallel.
Check which hosts match first with --list-hosts.
Prefer idempotent modules over `shell` so reruns are safe.
commands.explanation: Ansible ad-hoc commands run single module tasks against inventory hosts without writing a playbook. Useful for quick checks, one-time changes, and testing connectivity. The -m flag selects the module; -a passes arguments.
commands.pro_tip: Use `ansible all -m ping -i inventory.ini` as a connectivity health check before running playbooks — catches SSH key issues and unreachable hosts before they cause partial failures.

commands.name: ansible-playbook
commands.summary: Run Ansible playbooks to automate multi-host configuration.
commands.risk_reason: Playbooks run against real hosts; always use --check first.
cautions: Run with --check --diff --limit <host> first.
Without --limit the play targets every host matched by its hosts: pattern.
Use serial: and max_fail_percentage in the play to roll out gradually.
commands.explanation: ansible-playbook executes YAML playbooks that define desired state across managed hosts. Supports tags for selective execution, limits for targeting host subsets, and check mode for dry-run previews. The --diff flag shows exactly what files will change.

flags.desc: Only run tasks with these tags

examples.desc: Run only nginx and ssl tasks

safer.why: See which hosts would be targeted.

commands.pro_tip: Always run with `--check --diff` before the real run in production — it shows exactly what would change without risk. Add this as a required CI step before any production ansible run.

commands.name: terraform state
commands.summary: Inspect and manipulate Terraform state directly.
commands.risk_reason: State corruption can desync Terraform from real infrastructure.
cautions: State commands edit the source of truth for your infrastructure — a wrong `state rm` makes Terraform forget (and later recreate) real resources.
Always back up first: terraform state pull > backup.tfstate.
Prefer `moved` blocks or `import` blocks over manual state surgery.
commands.explanation: terraform state commands allow direct inspection and manipulation of the state file without modifying infrastructure. Essential for recovering from drift, importing existing resources, renaming resources, and resolving state conflicts.

examples.desc: List all resources tracked in state
Show detailed state for a specific resource
Rename a resource in state (after refactoring HCL)
Remove resource from state (stop managing, don't delete)
Import existing AWS resource into state

safer.why: Back up the state before any edit.

commands.pro_tip: Use `terraform state rm resource.name` to untrack a resource you want to keep but manage outside Terraform — safer than deleting the HCL config directly.

commands.name: terraform workspace
commands.summary: Manage multiple Terraform state workspaces for environment isolation.
commands.risk_reason: Wrong workspace can apply changes to the wrong environment.
cautions: Workspaces share one backend config — run `terraform workspace show` before apply or destroy.
`workspace delete` removes the state of that workspace while its real resources keep existing (orphaned).
commands.explanation: Terraform workspaces maintain separate state files for the same configuration, enabling environment isolation (dev/staging/prod) without duplicating code. Each workspace has its own state. The current workspace name is accessible via `terraform.workspace`.

examples.desc: Use workspace name to select var file

commands.pro_tip: Always run `terraform workspace show` before plan/apply in production — verify you're in the right workspace before making changes. Add it to your pre-apply checklist.

commands.name: terraform destroy
commands.risk_reason: Deletes every resource in the state — databases, networks, data.
cautions: Confirm workspace and backend first (terraform workspace show).
Resources with prevent_destroy or deletion protection are the last line of defence — do not remove them to “make it work”.
Back up data (snapshots) before destroying databases/volumes.
Never use -auto-approve outside disposable environments.
commands.explanation: Plans and removes all resources managed by the current configuration/workspace.

commands.name: terraform import
commands.risk_reason: Edits state; wrong address/ID attaches the wrong resource.
cautions: Back up state first; run terraform plan afterwards and fix drift before applying.
commands.explanation: Brings a real resource under Terraform management.

commands.explanation: Checks syntax and internal consistency. See the flags and examples below, and run `man terraform` for the full reference.

commands.name: terraform fmt

commands.name: terraform output
commands.risk_reason: Read-only; may print secrets.
cautions: Outputs can contain secrets unless marked sensitive.
commands.explanation: Prints root module outputs. See the flags and examples below, and run `man terraform` for the full reference.

commands.name: terraform taint
commands.risk_reason: The next apply destroys and recreates it.
cautions: Recreation can cause downtime and data loss.
commands.explanation: Deprecated; use terraform apply -replace.

commands.name: terraform force-unlock
commands.risk_reason: Removing an active lock can corrupt state if another apply is running.
cautions: Confirm nobody else is running terraform (CI too).
commands.explanation: Manually unlocks state. See the flags and examples below, and run `man terraform` for the full reference.

commands.name: terragrunt
commands.risk_reason: run-all applies across many modules.
cautions: run-all affects every module below the current directory.
Always run run-all plan first.
commands.explanation: Orchestrates multiple Terraform modules.

commands.risk_reason: User-data scripts run as root on first boot.
cautions: `cloud-init clean` makes the instance re-initialise at the next boot, possibly resetting SSH keys and hostname.
commands.explanation: Inspect cloud-init status and logs. See the flags and examples below, and run `man cloud-init` for the full reference.
